title: Geotechnical Risk Register
body: When operations treats the GT risk register as "geo's paperwork" instead of a live production constraint, equipment ends up working under walls that are actively being scaled or monitored for movement — that's how a rockfall hazard becomes a struck-by incident instead of a controlled closeout.
keyPoints: The register scores every hazard twice — before and after controls — on the same 1–5 scale as an IBRA. Nine of 29 original hazards started Extreme; after controls, only four stay at Medium residual risk (900-level crests and switchback joint-plane areas). Those four are still open — check them on a wall walk, don't assume "controlled" means "closed."

Two new hazards landed in the June update: HZ030 (Stage 4 catchment berm, not yet built — status "in progress") and HZ031 (fractured final wall, 780–770RL, scored Extreme — the first new Extreme hazard since the register was issued). Wall scaling on HZ031 is already underway.

The recurring controls are simple and repeatable: no-go/exclusion zones, 2 m bunds set back 15–20 m from the toe, no parking or stopping along the ramp or wall, and a spotter when mining near a no-go zone. If you see equipment parked tight against a wall with an open hazard, that's a direct control breach, not a judgment call.

Four systemic gaps (HZ009–HZ012) sit above individual hazards — missing geotechnical sign-off before mining, no post-scaling assessment, no final-wall acceptance form, and blast design that doesn't factor in geotech input. These are why hazards keep recurring instead of getting designed out.
apply: HZ031's wall scaling on 780–770RL sits directly above the 770-177 loading faces — if EX-123 or EX-253 are working that bench, confirm the exclusion zone below the wall is actually enforced, not just documented.
